To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“the reaction time of a nociceptive response to an increasing radiant heat stimulus is a function of the behavioral threshold, the behavioral latency, and the conduction speed of the peripheral fibers.”

(i) the behavioral threshold and latency are not the same as the thermal threshold and latency, (ii) the behavioral threshold is not the same as nociceptive threshold, (iii) the behavioral latency is not the same nociceptive latency, and (iv) the behavioral latency depends on the site of stimulation.

(1) the “tail-fick latency” (Tβ) is not a latency; (2) the behavioral latency (Tβ) depends on the initial skin temperature; (3) the behavioral latency is not a latency, but a threshold; (4) the reaction time is a function of the stimulus intensity; (5) the reaction time does not depend on the initial temperature of skin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a psychophysics of nociception, which is the first step towards a more complete understanding of pain.
the development and validation of a novel experimental paradigm and a psychophysical model for studying nociception and pain.
the behavioral and psychophysical determinants of the reaction time in the rat tail-flick response to noxious radiant heat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the “tail-fick” response to radiant heat is neither a pain response nor a simple reflex, but rather a complex behavior that depends on the interplay of peripheral and central determinants.

the reaction time of a tail-flick response to radiant heat does not represent a “pain index,” but rather a behavioral threshold that is determined by the temperature of the skin at the moment of the reaction.
the “tail-fick latency” is an unreliable index of nociception.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the behavioral TFL is an unreliable measure of nociception.
the reaction time of a tail-flick response is not a simple function of the temperature of radiant heat.
the “tail-fick latency” is a complex function of several parameters and that the use of this parameter for pain assessment is questionable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the “pain index” should not be based on the time elapsed between the beginning of heating and the reaction of the rat.
the behavioral response to radiant heat should not be considered a simple reflex, but rather as the outcome of a complex decision-making process.
the behavioral TFL is not a constant value but a variable that changes with the experimental conditions.
